concepts.def: Recurring theme attached to a character, place or idea, transformed in orchestration, harmony or tempo as the drama develops on screen.
Music that exists inside the story world and can be heard by the characters, such as a radio playing or an on-screen band.
Background score heard only by the audience, supporting dialogue and action by shaping mood without drawing attention to itself.
Scoring technique in which the music closely mimics on-screen movement, historically associated with animation and physical comedy.
Planning stage where director and composer watch the edit and decide exactly where each music cue should start, stop and peak.
Video-game scoring built from loops and layers that change in real time according to the player's location, actions and tension level.

walkthroughs.body_html:
Area of Study 3: Music for Media — a core area of A-Level Music.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Area of Study 3: Music for Media brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Area of Study 3: Music for Media.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: Music that the on-screen characters can themselves hear is described as what?
options: Non-diegetic
Diegetic
Underscore
Atonal

mcqs.q: A recurring theme associated with a particular character in a film score is called a what?
options: Cadenza
Leitmotif
Ostinato
Countermelody

mcqs.q: Music that precisely mirrors on-screen physical action is known as what?
options: Mickey-mousing
Spotting
Looping
Word-painting

mcqs.q: What makes video-game music different from most film music?
options: It never uses an orchestra
It must adapt in real time to the player's actions
It is always diegetic
It cannot use leitmotifs

mcqs.q: What makes a piece of music in a film 'diegetic'?
options: Diegetic means any music that was specially composed for the film.
A leitmotif may only ever be played by the brass section.
It exists inside the story world, so the characters can hear it - for example a song playing on a car radio.
Diegetic means music performed only on acoustic instruments.

mcqs.q: Does a leitmotif have to return in exactly the same form each time?
options: Underscore is always completely silent during dialogue.
No - composers vary its orchestration, harmony, tempo and mood so the theme reflects the changing drama.
A leitmotif must be repeated identically or the audience will not recognise it.
A leitmotif may only ever be played by the brass section.

mcqs.q: How prominent should underscore be during dialogue?
options: Underscore should be the loudest element so the audience notices the composer's work.
A leitmotif may only ever be played by the brass section.
Underscore is always completely silent during dialogue.
It usually sits low in the mix, supporting the mood without competing with the spoken words.
